claim: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on ImageNet classification can distinguish between stable and unstable block towers within a scenario with 60.1% accuracy.
source: These analyses replicated previous results by showing above chance classification accuracy within the Block Towers scenario and further found higher classification performance within our two new natural image sets (60.1%, 75%, and 71.4% for Block Towers, Physical-Objects, and Physical-People scenarios, respectively; diagonal cells in Figure 1B, p < 0.05 for a bootstrap test with n = 10,000).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CNN classification experiments reported in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CNNs trained on ImageNet classification can distinguish between stable and unstable Physical-Objects images with 75% accuracy within that scenario.
source: These analyses replicated previous results by showing above chance classification accuracy within the Block Towers scenario and further found higher classification performance within our two new natural image sets (60.1%, 75%, and 71.4% for Block Towers, Physical-Objects, and Physical-People scenarios, respectively; diagonal cells in Figure 1B, p < 0.05 for a bootstrap test with n = 10,000).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CNN classification experiments reported in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CNNs trained on ImageNet classification can distinguish between stable and unstable Physical-People images with 71.4% accuracy within that scenario.
source: These analyses replicated previous results by showing above chance classification accuracy within the Block Towers scenario and further found higher classification performance within our two new natural image sets (60.1%, 75%, and 71.4% for Block Towers, Physical-Objects, and Physical-People scenarios, respectively; diagonal cells in Figure 1B, p < 0.05 for a bootstrap test with n = 10,000).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from CNN classification experiments reported in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Visual features from ResNet-50 trained on ImageNet do not generalize across scenarios for physical stability classification.
source: However, this performance did not generalize across scenarios: accuracy was near chance for all cross-validation tests in which the SVM classifier was trained on one scenario and tested on a different scenario (i.e., off-diagonal cells in Figure 1B, p > 0.15 for a bootstrap test with n = 10,000).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing near-chance cross-scenario classification accuracy in CNN experiments.

claim: Visual features from VGG-16 trained on ImageNet do not carry abstract and generalizable information about physical stability across scenarios.
source: We also found similar results with a VGG-16 network trained on ImageNet.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from VGG-16 classification experiments.

claim: All participants had significant voxels within both ventral temporal cortex (VTC) and physics parcels.
source: All participants had significant voxels within both VTC and physics parcels (number of voxels per participant, mean ± standard error of the mean [SEM] =350.5 ± 68.7 for VTC ROIs and mean ± SEM =311.3 ± 69.8 for physics ROIs).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data collected from participants showing voxel counts in defined regions.

claim: VTC contains information about physical stability for Physical-Object scenarios as measured by multivoxel pattern analysis.
source: For VTC, we found that the within condition pattern correlations were significantly higher than the between condition pattern correlations for both Physical-Object and Physical-People scenarios (see Figure 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating the presence of information about stability for each scenario type.
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI multivoxel pattern analysis data showing significant differences in pattern correlations.

claim: VTC contains information about physical stability for Physical-People scenarios as measured by multivoxel pattern analysis.
source: For VTC, we found that the within condition pattern correlations were significantly higher than the between condition pattern correlations for both Physical-Object and Physical-People scenarios (see Figure 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating the presence of information about stability for each scenario type.
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI multivoxel pattern analysis data showing significant differences in pattern correlations.

claim: VTC pattern information does not distinguish perilous from nonperilous situations in the Animals-People scenarios.
source: However, pattern information did not distinguish perilous (or 'unstable') from nonperilous ('stable') situations in the Animals-People scenarios (see Figure 3 for stats).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI multivoxel pattern analysis data showing no significant differences for Animals-People scenarios.

claim: There is a significant interaction between scenario type and within versus between correlations in VTC (F1,12 = 72.2, p = 0.000002).
source: Further, this difference in stability information across scenario types was itself significant, as revealed by a significant interaction between-scenario type and within versus between correlations in an analysis of variance (ANOVA) (F1,12 = 72.2, p = 0.000002).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of fMRI pattern correlation data.

claim: The Physics Network contains information about physical stability for Physical-Object scenarios as measured by multivoxel pattern analysis.
source: The Physics Network showed the same pattern of results (Figures 2B and 3), with significantly higher correlations within than between stability for both the Physical-Object and Physical-People scenarios but not the Animals-People scenarios
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI multivoxel pattern analysis data showing significant differences in pattern correlations.

claim: The Physics Network contains information about physical stability for Physical-People scenarios as measured by multivoxel pattern analysis.
source: The Physics Network showed the same pattern of results (Figures 2B and 3), with significantly higher correlations within than between stability for both the Physical-Object and Physical-People scenarios but not the Animals-People scenarios
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI multivoxel pattern analysis data showing significant differences in pattern correlations.

claim: The Physics Network does not contain information distinguishing perilous from nonperilous situations in the Animals-People scenarios.
source: The Physics Network showed the same pattern of results (Figures 2B and 3), with significantly higher correlations within than between stability for both the Physical-Object and Physical-People scenarios but not the Animals-People scenarios
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI multivoxel pattern analysis data showing no significant differences for Animals-People scenarios.

claim: There is a significant interaction between scenario type and within versus between correlations in the Physics Network (F1,12 = 22.9, p = 0.0004).
source: and a significant ANOVA interaction between-scenario type and within versus between correlations (F1,12 = 22.9, p = 0.0004).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of fMRI pattern correlation data.

claim: The Physics Network shows patterns of response that generalize across Physical-Objects and Physical-People scenarios.
source: Indeed, we found that in the Physics Network (and not in VTC – see Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), the within condition pattern correlations are significantly higher than between condition pattern correlations only across Physical-Objects and Physical-People scenarios, but not across Physical and Animate scenarios (Figures 2D and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI cross-scenario multivoxel pattern analysis data.

claim: VTC does not show patterns of response that generalize across Physical-Objects and Physical-People scenarios.
source: Indeed, we found that in the Physics Network (and not in VTC – see Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), the within condition pattern correlations are significantly higher than between condition pattern correlations only across Physical-Objects and Physical-People scenarios, but not across Physical and Animate scenarios (Figures 2D and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI cross-scenario multivoxel pattern analysis data showing lack of generalization in VTC.

claim: There is a significant interaction between fROI (physics vs. VTC) and between-scenario stability information (F1,12 = 6.29, p = 0.027), indicating stronger generalization across scenarios in the Physics Network compared to VTC.
source: Further, we found a significant interaction between fROI (physics vs. VTC) and between-scenario stability information (within vs. between correlations), indicating stronger generalization across scenarios in the Physics Network compared to the VTC fROI (F1,12 = 6.29, p = 0.027).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) comparing fMRI pattern correlation data between regions.

claim: Saccade amplitude showed a significant difference between stable and unstable conditions in the Physical-People scenario (p = 0.028).
source: None of these quantities showed a significant difference between stable and unstable conditions in any of the scenarios except for saccade amplitude in the 'Physical-People' scenario (p = 0.028, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by eye-tracking data collected during fMRI scanning.

claim: There was no significant interaction of stability with scenario type for any eye movement quantities (p > 0.1).
source: However, we found no significant interaction of stability with scenario type for any of the eye movement quantities using separate ANOVAs (p > 0.1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of eye-tracking data.

claim: Unstable conditions received significantly higher interestingness ratings than stable conditions in all three scenarios (p < 0.001).
source: Second, analysis of subjective ratings by a separate set of subjects (see Methods) of 'interestingness' of our stimuli (which we used as a proxy for how attention-grabbing the stimuli were) revealed significantly higher ratings for unstable over stable conditions in all three scenarios (p < 0.001 for a paired t-test on average ratings across subjects; Supplementary file 1, last column).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral rating data from a separate experiment.

claim: The difference in interestingness ratings between stability conditions did not vary significantly between physical and animate scenarios (p = 0.23).
source: However, we found no interaction between stability and scenario type in the ANOVA (p = 0.23), implying that the difference in ratings between stability conditions did not vary between physical and animate scenarios.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of behavioral rating data.

claim: The generalization of stability information across Physical-Objects and Physical-People scenarios did not show a significant interaction with hemisphere (left vs. right; F1,12 = 2.75, p = 0.12).
source: An ANOVA analyzing the generalization of stability information (between vs. within condition pattern correlations across Physical-Objects and Physical-People; F1,12 = 6.11, p = 0.03 for the main effect) did not find a significant interaction of stability information with either hemisphere (left vs. right; F1,12 = 2.75, p = 0.12)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of fMRI data from subregions.

claim: The generalization of stability information across Physical-Objects and Physical-People scenarios did not show a significant interaction with lobe (parietal vs. frontal; F1,12 = 0.24, p = 0.63).
source: or lobe (parietal vs. frontal; F1,12 = 0.24, p = 0.63; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of fMRI data from subregions.

claim: V1 shows significant decoding of stability only in the Physical-Objects scenario but no cross-decoding of stability across physical scenarios.
source: In both regions, we found significant decoding of stability only in Physical-Objects scenario but no cross-decoding of stability across physical scenarios (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI multivoxel pattern analysis data from V1.

claim: LOC shows significant decoding of stability only in the Physical-Objects scenario but no cross-decoding of stability across physical scenarios.
source: In both regions, we found significant decoding of stability only in Physical-Objects scenario but no cross-decoding of stability across physical scenarios (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI multivoxel pattern analysis data from LOC.

claim: The interaction of cross-decoding effect with fROI was significant when contrasting the Physics Network with V1 (F1,12 = 6.31, p = 0.027).
source: In addition, the interaction of this cross-decoding effect with fROI was significant in separate ANOVAs contrasting the Physics Network with V1 (F1,12 = 6.31, p = 0.027)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) comparing fMRI pattern correlation data between regions.

claim: The interaction of cross-decoding effect with fROI was significant when contrasting the Physics Network with LOC (F1,12 = 5.63, p = 0.035).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) comparing fMRI pattern correlation data between regions.

claim: The Physics Network shows significantly greater response to physically unstable conditions compared to physically stable conditions in Physical-Objects scenarios (p = 0.02).
source: As predicted, the physically unstable condition showed a significantly greater response compared to the physically stable condition in both 'Physical-Objects' (p = 0.02 for a paired t-test on average response across subjects)
evidence: The claim is supported by univariate fMRI response data from the Physics Network.

claim: The Physics Network shows significantly greater response to physically unstable conditions compared to physically stable conditions in Physical-People scenarios (p = 0.04).
source: and 'Physical-People' scenarios (p = 0.04 for a paired t-test on average response across subjects; Figures 4 and 5, left column)
evidence: The claim is supported by univariate fMRI response data from the Physics Network.

claim: The Physics Network does not show significantly greater response to unstable conditions compared to stable conditions in Animals-People scenarios (p = 0.66).
source: but not the 'Animals-People' scenario (p = 0.66 for a paired t-test on average response across subjects; Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by univariate fMRI response data from the Physics Network.

claim: There is a significant interaction between stability (unstable vs. stable) and lobe (parietal vs. frontal) for Physical-Objects scenarios (F1,12 = 8.28, p = 0.014).
source: We found a significant interaction between stability (unstable vs. stable) and lobe (F1,12 = 8.28, p = 0.014) but not hemisphere (F1,12 = 3.04, p = 0.11) for the 'Physical-Objects' scenarios
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of univariate fMRI response data from subregions.

claim: There is a significant interaction between stability (unstable vs. stable) and lobe (parietal vs. frontal) for Physical-People scenarios (F1,12 = 8.53, p = 0.013).
source: and the same pattern for the 'Physical-People' scenario (stability × lobe: F1,12 = 8.53, p = 0.013; stability × hemisphere: F1,12 = 0.34, p = 0.57).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of univariate fMRI response data from subregions.

claim: There is a significant interaction of stability with region (physics fROI vs. V1) for Physical-Objects scenarios (F1,12 = 13.04, p = 0.0035).
source: Furthermore, we found a significant interaction of stability with region (physics fROI vs. visual fROI) for the 'Physical-Objects' (F1,12 = 13.04, p = 0.0035 for V1; F1,12 = 8.27, p = 0.014 for VTC)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) comparing univariate fMRI response data between regions.

claim: There is a significant interaction of stability with region (physics fROI vs. VTC) for Physical-Objects scenarios (F1,12 = 8.27, p = 0.014).
source: Furthermore, we found a significant interaction of stability with region (physics fROI vs. visual fROI) for the 'Physical-Objects' (F1,12 = 13.04, p = 0.0035 for V1; F1,12 = 8.27, p = 0.014 for VTC)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) comparing univariate fMRI response data between regions.

claim: There is a significant interaction of stability with region (physics fROI vs. LOC) for Physical-People scenarios (F1,12 = 7.83, p = 0.016).
source: and the 'Physical-People' scenarios (F1,12 = 11.14, p = 0.0059 for V1; F1,12 = 7.83, p = 0.016 for LOC).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) comparing univariate fMRI response data between regions.

claim: Visual motion area MT shows significantly higher responses for unstable/perilous than stable/safe scenes for all three types of scenarios.
source: As shown in Figures 3 and 5 (last column), we found significantly higher responses in MT for unstable/perilous than stable/safe scenes for all three types of scenarios without any significant stability information in the pattern activations.
evidence: The claim is supported by univariate fMRI response data from MT.

claim: MT does not show significant stability information in pattern activations across the three scenario types.
source: As shown in Figures 3 and 5 (last column), we found significantly higher responses in MT for unstable/perilous than stable/safe scenes for all three types of scenarios without any significant stability information in the pattern activations.
evidence: The claim is supported by multivoxel pattern analysis data from MT showing no significant pattern information.

claim: CNNs trained on ImageNet learn powerful representations that support not only object recognition, but multiple other tasks like object detection, segmentation, and retrieval.
source: Computational work has shown that convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on ImageNet learn powerful representations that support not only object recognition, but multiple other tasks like object detection, segmentation, and retrieval (Liu et al., 2015; Golub et al., 2020; Babenko et al., 2014; Razavian et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior computational studies.

claim: Several studies have claimed that CNNs can accurately predict scene stability.
source: Indeed, several studies have claimed that these networks can accurately predict scene stability (Lerer et al., 2016; Conwell et al., 2019; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies on CNN stability prediction.

claim: CNNs have so far been tested only within very narrow domains for stability prediction (e.g., block towers).
source: But CNNs have so far been tested only within very narrow domains (e.g., block towers with several cubes of different colors, in Figure 1A, left column) and it is not clear they would successfully predict future states of complex natural images (e.g., Figure 1A, middle two columns).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the literature review and comparison to the current study's stimuli.

claim: Human observers can perceive stability extremely rapidly and preattentively.
source: On the one hand, human observers can perceive the stability extremely rapidly and preattentively (Firestone and Scholl, 2017; Yang and Wolfe, 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Rapid and preattentive perception of stability has been taken to argue for a simple feedforward rather than a simulation process.
source: and these findings have been taken to argue for a simple feedforward rather than a simulation process.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cited literature about interpretations of rapid perception.

claim: Human judgments of the stability of a tower of blocks are well modeled by approximate probabilistic simulation in game-style physics engines.
source: On the other hand, human judgments of the stability of a tower of blocks are well modeled by approximate probabilistic simulation in game-style physics engines (Battaglia et al., 2013; Ullman et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2016; Gerstenberg et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior computational modeling studies.

claim: Physics engines better fit the human pattern of errors in stability judgments than CNNs do.
source: which better fit the human pattern of errors than CNNs do (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a prior comparative study.

claim: The ventral visual pathway has long been implicated in visual object recognition.
source: However, in frontoparietal regions previously implicated in intuitive physical reasoning we find both scenario-invariant representations of physical stability, and higher univariate responses to unstable than stable scenes. These results demonstrate abstract representations of physical stability in the dorsal but not ventral pathway, consistent with the hypothesis that the computations underlying stability entail not just pattern classification but forward physical simulation.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about the ventral visual pathway's role in object recognition.

claim: The ventral visual pathway is well modeled by CNNs trained on ImageNet.
source: One such region is the ventral visual pathway, which is widely thought to conduct the core computations underlying visual object recognition, and which is well modeled by CNNs trained on ImageNet (Yamins et al., 2014; Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies showing correspondence between CNNs and ventral pathway.

claim: Parietal and frontal regions have been shown to be engaged when people predict what will happen next in physical (more than social) scenarios.
source: However, an alternative hypothesis is that this information will be found instead in a set of parietal and frontal regions that have been shown to be engaged when people predict what will happen next in physical (more than social) scenarios (Fischer et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a prior fMRI study.

claim: Parietal and frontal regions hold information about physical variables such as mass, invariant to the scenario that revealed that mass.
source: and hold information about physical variables such as mass, invariant to the scenario that revealed that mass (Schwettmann et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a prior fMRI study on mass representation.

claim: If determining the stability of a scene requires an abstract representation of physical properties and forward simulation, then the Physics Network would be a more likely locus of these representations than the ventral visual pathway.
source: Thus, if determining the stability of a scene requires an abstract representation of the physical properties of the scene and the ability run forward simulations on those representations, then the Physics Network would be a more likely locus of these representations than the ventral visual pathway.
evidence: The claim is a logical inference based on the hypothesized computational requirements and known properties of brain regions.

claim: Simulations of unstable scenes where objects are expected to move require the construction and updating of dynamic representations that unfold over time.
source: That is, simulations of unstable scenes where objects are expected to move require the construction and updating of dynamic representations that unfold over time, whereas simulations of stable scenes, where objects are expected to remain stationary, do not require such dynamically updated representations.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference about the computational requirements of simulating different types of scenes.

claim: Simulations of stable scenes, where objects are expected to remain stationary, do not require dynamically updated representations.
source: That is, simulations of unstable scenes where objects are expected to move require the construction and updating of dynamic representations that unfold over time, whereas simulations of stable scenes, where objects are expected to remain stationary, do not require such dynamically updated representations.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference about the computational requirements of simulating different types of scenes.

claim: A higher univariate response to unstable than stable scenes would provide preliminary evidence for forward simulation.
source: Thus, a higher univariate response to unstable than stable scenes would provide preliminary (albeit not definitive) evidence for forward simulation.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference connecting predicted neural activity patterns to computational mechanisms.

claim: Participants were never asked to judge or think about the physical stability of the scenario they were viewing.
source: Importantly, participants were never asked to judge or think about the physical stability of the scenario they were viewing, which enabled us to ask whether this information is extracted even when not required by the task (Firestone and Scholl, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental design description.

claim: Visual features extracted by feedforward deep CNNs (like AlexNet, VGG, and ResNet) can distinguish between stable and unstable towers.
source: Previous studies have shown that visual features extracted by feedforward deep CNNs (like AlexNet, Ferrari et al., 2018; VGG, Li et al., 2016; and ResNet, Lerer et al., 2016; Conwell et al., 2019) can distinguish between stable and unstable towers.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies on CNN stability classification.

claim: CNN features produced above chance classification performance within a scenario (i.e., train on towers with two blocks and test on towers with four blocks).
source: Although these features produced above chance classification performance within a scenario (i.e., train on towers with two blocks and test on towers with four blocks), they have not been tested on very different scenarios and hence their ability to represent an abstract and generalizable notion of physical stability remains unknown.
evidence: The claim is based on citation to prior studies and inference about their limitations.

claim: The discriminative features underlying CNN stability discrimination within scenarios might be related to incidental properties that are indicative of stability only within a particular scenario.
source: The fact that these CNN features can distinguish stability within a scenario but not across scenarios suggests that the discriminative features underlying this discrimination might be related to incidental properties that are indicative of stability only within a particular scenario (e.g., the displacement of each block from the centroid of the block below).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed pattern of CNN performance.

claim: Brain regions optimized for visual object recognition tasks (ventral temporal cortex) might fail to contain scenario-invariant information about physical stability.
source: This result further suggests that brain regions thought to be optimized (through development and/or evolution) for similar tasks (ventral temporal cortex) might similarly fail to contain scenario-invariant information about physical stability
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the CNN results to predictions about brain regions.

claim: The human ability to judge physical stability may result from different kinds of representations in frontoparietal cortical regions previously implicated in physical inference.
source: and that the human ability to perform this task may result from different kinds of representations elsewhere in the brain, such as the frontoparietal cortical regions previously implicated in physical inference.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from CNN results and prior knowledge about brain regions involved in physical inference.

claim: Thirteen subjects (ages 21–34; 6 females and 7 males) participated in the fMRI experiment.
source: Thirteen subjects (ages 21–34; 6 females and 7 males) participated in the experiment which was cut short due to COVID-19 pandemic.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the experimental participants.

claim: All participants were right handed and had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
source: All participants were right handed and had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about participant characteristics.

claim: The stimulus set included 14 images for each condition in each scenario.
source: The stimulus set included 14 images for each condition in each scenario.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the experimental stimuli.

claim: All images were scaled so that the longer dimension measured 8° on the projector screen placed ~136 cm from the participant.
source: All images were scaled so that the longer dimension measured 8° on the projector screen places ~136 cm from the participant.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about stimulus presentation parameters.

claim: Images were chosen such that stability decoding accuracy was close to chance both within and across scenarios on features extracted from initial layers of a deep CNN.
source: We chose images from each of these six experimental conditions such that stability decoding accuracy was close to chance both within the scenario and also across scenarios on features extracted from the initial layers of a deep CNN.
evidence: The claim describes the image selection procedure based on CNN screening.

claim: Classification accuracies on pool_1 features from VGG-16 were close to chance for all three scenarios (42.9%, 53.6%, and 42.9% for Physical-Objects, Physical-People, and Animals-People scenarios, respectively).
source: The classification accuracies were close to chance (=50%) for all three scenarios (% accuracy: 42.9%, 53.6%, and 42.9% for Physical-Objects, Physical-People, and Animals-People scenarios, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by CNN classification data used for stimulus screening.

claim: Cross-decoding performance on pool_1 features from VGG-16 was close to chance (average accuracy = 51.8% for Physical-Objects vs. Physical-People, 44.6% for Physical-Objects vs. Animals-People, and 41.1% for Physical-People vs. Animals-People).
source: Here also, we found close to chance (=50%) cross-decoding performance (average % accuracy = 51.8% for Physical-Objects vs. Physical-People, 44.6% for Physical-Objects vs. Animals-People, and 41.1% for Physical-People vs. Animals-People).
evidence: The claim is supported by CNN cross-decoding data used for stimulus screening.

claim: Subjects found high arousal IAPS images more interesting than low arousal IAPS images (avg rating: high arousal = 3.5, low arousal = 1.5; p < 0.000005).
source: To validate this measure, we also included high and low arousal images (n = 14 each) from IAPS (Lang et al., 1997) and obtained higher interestingness ratings for high arousal images compared to low arousal IAPS images (avg interestingness rating: high arousal images = 3.5 and low arousal images = 1.5; p < 0.000005).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral rating data validating the interestingness measure.

claim: Each participant performed two runs of an 'intuitive physics' fMRI localizer task.
source: Each participant performed two runs of an 'intuitive physics' fMRI localizer task previously used to functionally define the frontoparietal physics engine in the brain (Fischer et al., 2016; Schwettmann et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: The physics localizer task used movies depicting unstable towers made of blue, yellow and white blocks created using Blender 2.70.
source: In this task, subjects viewed short movies (~6 s) depicting unstable towers made of blue, yellow and white blocks (see Figure 1A) created using Blender 2.70 (Blender Foundation).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the localizer stimuli.

claim: Each participant performed four runs of the main stability experiment.
source: In addition to the physics ROI localizer, each participant also performed four runs of the main experiment.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: Each run of the stability experiment contained 3 rest/fixation blocks and 12 20-s stimulus blocks (2 blocks for each of the 6 experimental conditions).
source: Each run of this experiment contained 3 rest/fixation blocks and 12 20-s stimulus blocks (2 blocks for each of the 6 experimental conditions).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Each image block in the stability experiment contained 10 trials including 2 1-back trials.
source: Each image block contained 10 trials including 2 1-back trials.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: In each trial of the stability experiment, an image was shown for 1.8 s followed by 0.2 s of fixation-only interval.
source: In each trial, an image was shown for 1.8 s followed by 0.2 s of fixation-only interval.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about trial timing.

claim: Activations from the fc1000 layer of ResNet-50 trained on ImageNet were extracted for stability classification analysis.
source: Activations from the fc1000 layer (fully connected layer just preceding the softmax layer) of a Resnet-50 model trained on ImageNet object recognition challenge were extracted for both stable and unstable conditions across Block Towers, Physical-Objects, and Physical-People scenarios.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the CNN analysis method.

claim: The Block Towers set used for CNN analysis contained 258 images each for stable and unstable conditions.
source: and the Block Towers set (n = 258 each for stable and unstable conditions) was used to replicate and extend earlier findings.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the stimulus set size.

claim: Eye movement data were recorded from 6 of the 13 subjects during the fMRI experiment using the EyeLink 1,000 Eye-Tracker.
source: Eye movement data were recorded from 6 of the 13 subjects during both the physics ROI localizer task and the stability experiment using the EyeLink 1,000 Eye-Tracker (SR Research) inside the scanner.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about eye-tracking data collection.

claim: Group-level physics parcels were derived from localizer data in 27 subjects using the Group-constrained Subject-Specific method.
source: We derived group-level physics parcels from the localizer data (Schwettmann et al., 2019) in 27 subjects using the Group-constrained Subject-Specific method described previously (Julian et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the parcel definition method.

claim: The group-level physics parcel derivation resulted in seven parcels spanning frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes.
source: This resulted in seven group-level parcels spanning frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the parcellation results.

claim: Two of the seven parcels in the occipital cortex were rejected because they were shown to respond to both physical and social stimuli.
source: We rejected two of the seven parcels in the occipital cortex since they were shown to respond to both physical and social stimuli (Fischer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about parcel selection based on prior findings.

claim: fROIs were defined in each individual subject as the intersection of subject-specific localizer contrast map and group-level (or anatomical) parcels.
source: We defined fROI in each individual subject as the intersection of subject-specific localizer contrast map and group-level (or anatomical) parcels.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the fROI definition method.

claim: The physics fROI was defined using an uncorrected p value < 0.001 for the physics > color contrast.
source: Specifically, we used the physics localizer to identify brain regions in each individual subject that responded more to the physics task compared to the color task (uncorrected p value <0.001 for the physics > color contrast).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the statistical threshold used for fROI definition.

claim: V1, LOC, and VTC fROIs were defined using an uncorrected p value < 0.001 for the physics + color > fixation contrast.
source: As before, we used data from the physics localizer to identify brain regions that responded to visual stimuli compared to fixation (uncorrected p value <0.001 for physics + color > fixation contrast).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the statistical threshold used for visual fROI definition.

claim: Area MT was localized using a standard localizer with coherent vs. random dot motion contrast.
source: In addition, we also localized area MT using a standard localizer (coherent vs. random dot motion contrast) (Tootell et al., 1995)
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the MT localizer method with citation to prior work.

claim: Pattern correlations were computed between voxel activation patterns for even and odd runs to avoid obscuring pattern information from temporal pattern drifts.
source: Note that by always comparing data across even and odd runs we avoid obscuring pattern information from temporal pattern drifts (Alink et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is a statement about methodological rationale with citation to prior work.

claim: MT has been previously reported to show greater response for static images with implied motion.
source: This increased response to conditions with predicted motion is reminiscent of previous reports showing greater response in MT for static images with implied motion (Kourtzi and Kanwisher, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a prior study on MT responses to implied motion.

claim: The current study shows activation of MT for motion that is only predicted (in the Physical-Objects and Physical-People scenarios).
source: The critical difference, however, is that whereas the earlier study reported higher responses in MT for static images depicting motion events happening at the moment the photograph was taken (implied motion) the current study shows activation of MT for motion that is only predicted (in the Physical-Objects and Physical-People scenarios).
evidence: The claim contrasts current findings with prior work, based on the experimental data.

claim: Similar frontoparietal regions have been shown to respond more during physics-based tasks compared to color-based or social prediction tasks.
source: Across multiple studies, similar frontoparietal regions have been shown to (1) respond more during physics-based tasks compared to color-based or social prediction tasks (Fischer et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a prior fMRI study.

claim: Frontoparietal regions have been shown to represent physical concepts in verbal stimuli.
source: (2) represent physical concepts in verbal stimuli (Mason and Just, 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Frontoparietal regions have been shown to contain scenario-invariant representations of object mass.
source: and (3) contain scenario-invariant representations of object mass (Schwettmann et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a prior fMRI study.

claim: The regions activated during physical inference overlap with regions engaged during visually guided action.
source: Intriguingly, the regions activated during physical inference overlap with regions shown previously to be engaged during visually guided action (Goodale and Westwood, 2004) and tool use (Gallivan et al., 2013; Valyear et al., 2007; Mruczek et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies on action and tool use.

claim: Physical simulation has been proposed as a crucial component in models for human-like robotic action planning.
source: Indeed physical simulation has been proposed as a crucial component in models for human-like robotic action planning (Toussaint et al., 2018; Toussaint et al., 2020; Mordatch et al., 2012) and flexible tool use (Allen et al., 2020; Osiurak and Badets, 2016; Osiurak et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior computational modeling work.

claim: The Physics Network overlaps with the 'multiple demand' system and is unlikely to be selectively engaged in only physical inference.
source: Note however that these same regions also overlap with the 'multiple demand' system (Fischer et al., 2016), and are unlikely to be selectively engaged in only physical inference.
evidence: The claim is based on citation to prior work and inference about functional specificity.

claim: Some work has shown that CNNs can learn from extensive labeled datasets to infer the stability of block towers.
source: Some work has shown that CNNs can learn from extensive labeled datasets to infer the stability of block towers (Lerer et al., 2016; Conwell et al., 2019) and predict future outcomes (Lerer et al., 2016; Conwell et al., 2019; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior computational studies.

claim: A general ability to predict what will happen next in physical scenarios will require a more structured representation of the physical world that will support forward simulation.
source: Instead, it has been proposed that a general ability to predict what will happen next in physical scenarios will require a more structured representation of the physical world that will support forward simulation (Battaglia et al., 2013; Ullman et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical and computational work.

claim: There is a debate in cognitive science between those who argue that rapid physical inferences are computed by pattern recognition versus those who argue for mental simulation.
source: A parallel debate is raging in cognitive science (Lerer et al., 2016; Conwell et al., 2019; Battaglia et al., 2013; Firestone and Scholl, 2017; Firestone and Scholl, 2016; Ludwin-Peery et al., 2019; Davis and Marcus, 2015; Chater and Oaksford, 2017; Davis et al., 2017; Ludwin-Peery et al., 2020), between those who argue that because human physical inferences occur rapidly (Firestone and Scholl, 2017) and preattentively (Firestone and Scholl, 2017) they are computed by something like a pattern recognition process, versus those who argue that human and primate physical inference behavior is best accounted for by mental simulation (Battaglia et al., 2013; Ullman et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2016; Gerstenberg et al., 2017; Rajalingham et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies representing different positions in the debate.

claim: Visual information represented in the ventral visual cortex is used by the Physics Network for efficient inference of physical properties.
source: We therefore hypothesize that visual information represented in the ventral visual cortex is used by the Physics Network for efficient inference of physical properties (see Almeida et al., 2013; Kravitz et al., 2011 for the cases of tool processing and visuospatial reasoning)
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the current findings and citations to related prior work.

claim: An integrated computational model has been proposed that uses visual representations from a deep-learning-based inverse graphics model to initialize simulations in a physics-engine-based generative model.
source: This idea has been recently proposed as an integrated computational model that uses visual representations from a deep-learning-based inverse graphics model to initialize simulations in a physics-engine-based generative model of object dynamics, which then can be used to perceive, predict, reason about, and plan with physical objects (Yildirim et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior computational modeling work.

claim: Models with flexible, object-centric representations and the ability to learn from realistic visual inputs should be able to make predictions of physical stability on realistic stimuli.
source: This class of models with flexible, object-centric representations and the ability to learn from realistic visual inputs (Bear, 2020; Mrowca, 2018) should be able to make predictions of physical stability on the realistic stimuli used in our experiment and also form the basis for neurally mappable encoding models of the candidate physics regions.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on inference from model properties and citations to relevant computational work.

claim: The question of how an integrated vision-physics model is instantiated in the brain remains unanswered.
source: The question of how such a model is instantiated, if at all, in the brain remains unanswered and provides a fertile avenue for future exploration.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the current state of knowledge and future research directions.

claim: Our mental physics engine may compress rich visual details into a relatively small number of individual objects and associated events for efficient approximation.
source: According to one hypothesis, our mental physics engine compresses the rich details in our visual world into a relatively small number of individual objects and associated events in order to efficiently generate a reasonable approximation of the scene at the spatial and temporal scales relevant to human perception and action (Ullman et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis supported by citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: Abstractions in mental physics may enable us to run simulations faster than real time with compressed timescales (like hippocampal replay).
source: These abstractions may also enable us to run simulations faster than real time with compressed timescales (like hippocampal replay, Lee and Wilson, 2002), enabling us to make rapid and accurate predictions of the consequences of multiple actions under consideration, including our ability to make fast and automatic physical inference (Firestone and Scholl, 2017; Firestone and Scholl, 2016).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on analogy to hippocampal replay and citations to relevant work.
